amyloid imaging and cortical thickness are more suitable to detect progression of disease in early AD compared to FDG PET.
amyloid PET and MRI cortical thickness are more suitable to detect progression of disease in early AD than FDG PET.

amyloid PET is superior to FDG-PET and cortical thickness MRI to detect progression of AD in a small sample size.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
amyloid deposition is the strongest biomarker of disease progression in early Alzheimer's disease and the most powerful imaging marker to track progression.
the choice of the most sensitive biomarker depends on the expected effect size of a treatment and that the choice of a biomarker should be considered carefully.

The main takeaway from our work is that
amyloid imaging is the most powerful biomarker for detecting disease progression in early Alzheimer's disease, followed by cortical thickness, while FDG PET is the least powerful biomarker.
the choice of the biomarker to use in trials of disease modifying drugs should be based on effect size and sample size.
longitudinal studies should be powered for effect size and not for statistical power alone.
